cite: In re Herse, 2 Liquor Tax Rep. 256
holding_summary: Proceeding to revoke a liquor tax certificate for failure to obtain consents of two-thirds of dwelling owners within 200 feet; case only construes how the 200-foot distance to nearby dwellings is measured.
notes: Concerns liquor-license consent distance rules for nearby dwellings; no letting of rooms/lodging arrangement at issue.

cite: Thompson v. Fort Miller Pulp & Paper Co., 14 Misc. 477
holding_summary: Riparian rights dispute over a dam flooding plaintiff's farm; damages awarded, injunction withheld.
notes: Dam/riparian-rights case; no occupancy or lodging issue.

holding_summary: Plaintiff denied injunction against defendant's building-restriction violation because plaintiff had himself violated the same setback covenant.
notes: Building-restriction covenant dispute between neighboring homeowners; no letting/lodging arrangement.

cite: In re Judicial Settlement of the Account of Walsh, 126 Misc. 479
holding_summary: Executor accounting proceeding addressing an executor's self-dealing profit on sale of estate realty, rent-collection commissions, and whether the widow's will provisions were in lieu of dower.
notes: Estate accounting/dower case; executors' general power to lease estate realty is mentioned only as part of the will-construction analysis, not a lodging/short-term letting dispute.

cite: Rochester Yacht Club Co. v. Rochester Boat Works, Inc., 126 Misc. 309
holding_summary: Plaintiff could not enforce a residential building-restriction covenant against a boat-manufacturing plant where plaintiff itself held unrestricted lots and knew of the changed restriction scheme.
notes: Restrictive-covenant/commercial-use dispute; no dwelling-letting or lodging issue.

holding_summary: Mandamus to compel a public-garage permit denied because the city ordinance regulating (among other things) livery/boarding stables and public garages was invalid for lack of charter authority.
notes: Ordinance regulates livestock 'boarding... stables' and public garages, not human lodging/boarding houses; irrelevant despite selector match on 'boarding'.

holding_summary: Certiorari upholding a zoning board of appeals' grant of a permit to build a garage extending into a residential district in connection with an apartment house.
notes: Zoning dispute over an accessory garage for an apartment house; no lodging/boarding issue.

holding_summary: Mandamus denied to compel a building permit for an apartment house in a residential zone; zoning ordinance prohibiting apartment houses on the street held constitutional.
notes: Zoning exclusion of multi-family apartment houses from a residential street; concerns permanent apartment buildings, not room-letting or boarding houses.

cite: Hecht-Dann Construction Co. v. Burden, 124 Misc. 632
holding_summary: Peremptory mandamus granted to compel a building permit; zoning ordinance's arbitrary zone line and 25-foot setback requirement held unreasonable and void as applied to the lot.
notes: Zoning setback-line validity dispute; no lodging/letting issue.

holding_summary: Riparian-rights case over filled-in land adjacent to plaintiff's upland; injunction against building on the fill granted and title to upland fixed as of 1920.
notes: Riparian/accretion dispute; no occupancy or letting issue.

cite: Orville Realty Co. v. Warnick, 113 Misc. 346
court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term
holding_summary: A realty company let a summer cottage to a tenant under successive written leases running only May to November; when the company sought use-and-occupation rent for the following winter, the court refused to imply a renewed tenancy, holding that the seasonal, short-term character of the letting and the parties' actual conduct controlled over any rigid holdover-renewal rule.

quotes.text: The defendant for years had been occupying the property in question during the summer months under written leases from plaintiff’s predecessor, and continued that course after 1916, when the plaintiff acquired the property.

Where, however, from the terms of the lease or the conduct of the parties some continuance of the tenancy beyond the original term has been contemplated, so that a holding over is not wrongful, or other circumstances demonstrate that both parties contemplate something other than an implied continuance of the term, the implication necessarily yields to the actual facts.
For the reasons stated, the judgment should be reversed, with thirty dollars costs, and the complaint dismissed, with costs.

notes: Whole-cottage seasonal letting by a realty company, not a householder letting rooms in an occupied dwelling; included because it treats short-term seasonal letting as governed by the parties' actual intent rather than an artificial year-long implication, favoring freedom to let short-term.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term
holding_summary: A landlord's stay of eviction was vacated where the tenant used a cottage for both dwelling and his express business, casting doubt on whether the emergency Housing Laws applied at all.
notes: Ordinary long-term month-to-month tenancy of a mixed dwelling/business cottage; not a lodging or short-term room-letting arrangement.

cite: 810 West End Avenue, Inc. v. Frankel, 113 Misc. 338
court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term
holding_summary: Summary dispossess proceeding turning on whether a grantee of an apartment building could recover rent that accrued before it acquired title, absent a valid assignment.
notes: Technical rent-assignment/apportionment dispute between successive apartment-building owners and a tenant; no lodging or room-letting issue.

cite: Ullmann Realty Co. v. Tamur, 113 Misc. 538
holding_summary: Upholding the constitutionality of New York's 1920 emergency Housing Laws suspending ejectment of holdover apartment tenants who pay reasonable rent, the court sustained the statute as a valid police-power response to the housing shortage, while noting the legislation was addressed specifically to ordinary dwelling houses where people make permanent homes, not to hotels and rooming houses occupied mainly by transient guests.

quotes.text: In an action of ejectment by the owner of a dwelling house in the city of New York in which the defendant, a monthly tenant from September 24, 1918, occupied an apartment, the complaint alleged that since September 24, 1920, defendant has withheld possession of the premises from plaintiff

Obviously no extensive discussion is required to point out the distinction between the ordinary dwelling house where persons make their permanent homes and hotels and rooming houses, mainly occupied by transient guests. The one is not comparable in importance, so far as it is a matter of public concern, to the other. The evil aimed at had its root in the one. To it alone the legislature properly addressed its attention.

notes: Polarity marked mixed: the case sustains broad rent-eviction regulation of ordinary apartment dwellings (adverse-leaning use of police power) but expressly excludes rooming houses/hotels serving transient guests from that regulatory reach, articulating the permanent-dwelling vs. transient-lodging distinction central to this corpus.

holding_summary: Injunction pendente lite denied because a fire escape projecting into a restricted front setback does not violate a covenant against erecting 'buildings' in that space.
notes: Restrictive-covenant/fire-escape dispute; no occupancy or letting issue.

cite: Marbridge Building Co. v. White, 113 Misc. 210
holding_summary: Landlord recovered damages from a holdover office tenant (a dentist) whose failure to timely vacate delayed a new tenant's possession, plus counsel fees from the prior summary proceeding.
notes: Commercial office holdover-damages dispute, not a dwelling; no lodging issue.

holding_summary: Demurrer overruled; the 1920 Housing Law barring ouster of dwelling-house tenants who pay reasonable rent, absent specified exceptions, held a valid exercise of the police power.
notes: General housing-law constitutionality ruling for an ordinary apartment tenancy; unlike Ullmann v. Tamur in this same batch, it contains no discussion of lodging/rooming houses or transient occupancy, so it does not bear on the corpus's specific doctrinal question.

holding_summary: In a proceeding to revoke a liquor tax certificate for lack of required dwelling-owner consents, the court held that a householder who occasionally lets rooms by the week to outsiders does not thereby convert his house into a boardinghouse or place of business; it remains a private dwelling entitled to the privacy and protections of that status.

quotes.text: it appears that the owner of one of the houses was in the habit of letting rooms by the week to persons who might apply for them, and it is claimed by the respondent that this action constituted .him a boardinghouse keeper, under the law, and that he was carrying on a business within the meaning of the statute.
The fact that one or more of his rooms were let for occupancy of persons other than members of his family would not deprive his house of its character as a dwelling-house.

It is not a place where the general public would be invited to enter and transact business, but for every intent it would still be a private house, and its occupants entitled to the privacy which surrounds a dwelling-house.
